utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I understand from the registrar that there is a difficulty about the witness list, which has not been transmitted to you. If that's so, it's obviously something we should look into, but what we will do is we will hear the witness now that the witness is here, and we'll look into those matters when his evidence is over or at a convenient time during it. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Perhaps you could look into this matter of the witness list. One was apparently promised but has not been sent. In any event, we'll hear about it in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I would like to stress that the witness is under a certain time constraint and, therefore, we would suggest that all procedural matters be discussed after we heard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is normally my practice, as you will have seen, to discuss procedural matters when the witness is finished. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: He has to be sworn in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not even a procedural matter; it is a question of a correct attitude. I have no information as to who the next witness will be after Mr. Okun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Milosevic, I'm not going to interrupt you further, but we will deal with that later in the day. Let us hear the witness first. Yes. If you'd take the declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: My name is Colm Mangan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are the chief of the defence staff of the Irish national defence force?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your rank?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: My rank is Lieutenant General.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were a team leader of the European Community Monitoring Mission in Croatia in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I was a member of the monitoring mission, and at times I performed the duties of team leader, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When exactly were you in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: From July 1991 until the end of January 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly summarise the mandate and duties of the ECMM and yourself.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: We went to the area initially to monitor the cease-fire arrangements in the Federal Republic of Slovenia, and thereafter we became involved in the monitoring of the ongoing conflict in the Federal Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In March 2001, you gave a statement to the OTP that you did review yesterday and confirmed in a legal proceeding with an addendum; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would like to tender this 92 bis statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 399, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: There is the addendum, Your Honours. The addendum is at tab 9.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the addendum that you corrected, you corrected a reference in paragraph 8 and 9 of your statement in relation to Dr. Milan Babic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These paragraphs, 8 and 9 of your statement, do they deal with the cease-fire negotiation in September 1991 in the Osijek region?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were present?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I was present for a short period in that location, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person you met as the chief negotiator on the Serb side, how was he introduced to you, and who was he?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: He was introduced to me as the Minister for Agriculture in the Republic of Baranja, Srem, and Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you had a discussion in preparation of your testimony, did you review a list of ministries and officials in this SAO Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to avoid to put it to the witness again. It's Exhibit 327, tab 6. We have discussed this list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see there the Minister of Agriculture listed with the name Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a recollection of this person and this name?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: The man that we were negotiating with was the Minister for Agriculture at that time and not the man I originally stated, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever meet Dr. Milan Babic, the president of the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: No, I didn't meet him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you gave your statement, did you also provide copies of several ECMM reports as attachments?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These reports, do they deal with the overall situation in Croatia, including Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: They do, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where and by whom were such documents drafted?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: The documents were drafted by a number of people who were working at the tasking cell. That was at the headquarters of the mission in Zagreb. They received reports from the various teams that were operating throughout the country, and they consolidated those reports at the headquarters, and they were then transmitted in the form of a report to The Hague. It was the Dutch presidency at the time. These reports were a consolidation of the reports that were made by the various teams that were operating throughout Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, the tab numbers are tab 1 to tab 8, and they are actually listed in the proofing summary, and we would like to tender the proofing summary and have it marked as -- marked for identification, not as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you want the reports to be exhibited, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would it not be convenient simply to exhibit those reports? They are attached to the statement. Can we discuss this with the registrar about a convenient way to deal with it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There's one issue arising, and that was the missing document RMCM01 which Your Honour will remember we didn't have when we dealt with the 92 bis written argument. It's attachment 1. Within that, in the second half, there's a section called "Monitoring Experiences in Yugoslavia," and I've noted from the additional statement provided by the witness for these proceedings today that there is a disclaimer as to that part of the evidence, that it's anything that he had written or to do with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we note the disclaimer. We can take that into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps it should be taken out of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will discuss this attachment in particular with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll hear about it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the attachments will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 400.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were in Zagreb, did the ECMM get information that the JNA were preparing an attack on Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: We received information from the Croat authorities that this -- that Dubrovnik was threatened, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your reaction to this information?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I have to say that we were disinclined to believe it at that stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: Because all of the activities of the JNA before that time had been in support of the indigenous Serb population, and we were aware that there were no or very few Serbs in Dubrovnik, and consequently, we didn't consider that the JNA would be threatening the city of Dubrovnik because we couldn't see any reason for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Dubrovnik have any military significance that you could see?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: Not that we could see, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was an ECMM team with the name Whisky dispatched to Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: They were the first team that were dispatched to Dubrovnik to check the reports that we were receiving of the city under threat.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to put to the witness tab 1 of Exhibit 400.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's actually several documents included here. The first document, with the headline "Visit by Team Whisky," is that the report of this team, the first team that went there?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: That's a report of the team, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the second last paragraph on the first page, there is a reference to a press conference of this team appealing in the name of the EC mission for those concerned to desist at once from these apparently unprovoked attacks. Are you aware of this press conference or this --

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I am aware that that was the opinion of that team who were in Dubrovnik at that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the second page, in the first paragraph, there is a reference made to extraneous attempts to contact the JNA directly but without success. Were you aware that that was the situation?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: When we took over from that team, we were aware that was the situation. They so informed us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the middle of the second page there is a reference to the successor team, Charlie. Would that be your team?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you would please now turn to the next document that is part of this same exhibit. It's with the headline, "Subject: Visit to Dubrovnik on the 29th of October, 1991." Were you aware that ambassadors, politicians went there on that day?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: We were aware of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I would like to quote from the first paragraph. It says here: "Although physical damage to the old city centre is slight, the direct surroundings of Old Dubrovnik shows random shelling, damage to streets, houses and cars that can only serve one purpose; psychological warfare on the civilian population in order to empty Dubrovnik of its people. The party received information about far more extensive damage to the villages immediately surrounding Dubrovnik for which there seemed to be no military need either." Was that the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we ask counsel to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the prevailing opinion at that time?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you now please turn to page 3 of this same Dubrovnik visit document, and in the last paragraph, it says here: "All members of the party, including those with military expertise, agreed that no conceivable military purpose could be served by either destroying the city or emptying it of its civilian population of which there still are tens of thousands around." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Could you comment on this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: That would have been not only the views of those who were on that visit but it would have been widely held also within the ECMM at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your own view?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: That would have coincided with my view, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I would like you to turn now to the next document which is called monitoring experience in Yugoslavia. Could you comment on this document without going into the details?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I would just make one comment, and as you have seen in my disclaimer, it was contained in the bulk of reports that I submitted, but it is not a report. It's a highly personalised individual account and is not one of the official reports. I don't know who wrote it, and I don't know the origin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Having read the first sentence, I don't think it would be right to put it in.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I do not insist on putting it in. It was just the -- this group of documents that were provided during the statement and -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will have it out. We will remove it from the bundle.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you turn to the next document that belongs to that same exhibit, it's called "Name Doc Dubrovnik," and I would like to quote to you from page 1, paragraph 3: "The process at work in Dubrovnik, Dalmatia, and along the other frontlines is one of deliberate intimidation. The purpose is not necessarily occupation, which the JNA now seems increasingly unlikely to sustain; but it is certainly depopulation. To drive Croatians out of the agricultural and economic heartlands of Dalmatia and Slavonia, wreaking havoc with their economy and leaving them no homes to return to if, in any event, the JNA do withdraw. A deliberate scorched earth policy." Could you comment on this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: That paragraph is, as I said, put together in the headquarters in Zagreb, and it would have been a distillation of the reports of various teams working in the area, but that would have given a good sense of the type of report that was being delivered by the teams working in Croatia at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I would like to quote also from paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters don't have the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The interpreters don't have the documents, they say, so have you got a copy for them? Oh, they apparently do.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: They should have it. I'm just told it should be under tab 1.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The English booth has the document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And it's an English document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let's see how we get on. Perhaps you if you are going to read, could you do it slowly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I quote now from paragraph 4. It begins with -- it's about a pattern that is described here as such. It begins with: "Limited fire, such as mortars, giving civilians the chance to escape with minimal casualties. Then it escalates to tanks and artillery to destroy the abundant villages more systematically." And after some details, it then continues: "These are the intentional product of this war, which explains incidentally why the JNA are often keen to 'help' evacuate civilians, and the Croatians sometimes reluctant to agree, vide Ilok." Could you comment on these quotes that I just put to you.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: That would be consistent with the nature of reports that were being made from the EC mission in Zagreb at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened in Ilok? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: That was at the town of Ilok which was in Eastern Slavonia, and it had been cut off in an occupied area but had not been subjected to any shelling or destruction during the fighting in Eastern Slavonia. The village was then evacuated by consent with the mayor of Ilok. The Croatian authorities were somewhat disturbed by that, that the ECMM had assisted in the evacuation of the village in that they were assisting in the removal of the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And further down there is a paragraph on Dubrovnik, speaking of indiscriminate -- indiscriminate shelling and -- directed against civilian targets. Is that something you --

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: That is correct. Indiscriminate insofar as that there were no apparent military targets that would have been -- one would have discriminated to take them on. So the targets were indiscriminate in that sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. This would conclude this document. I would like now to turn to paragraph 17 of the statement, and it refers to weapons used and your observations in Sokar [phoen]. During your time in Dubrovnik, was the town shelled from land, air, and sea?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: That's correct, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many air attacks did you observe?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I would have observed one air attack, a naval bombardment, and a number of mortar and artillery attacks on the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in which time period was that, approximately?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: That was approximately the period from the 5th of October, 1991, to the 7th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you observed this naval attack, what did -- what was the target, and what did you see?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: The target was the Hotel Excelsior, which is just to the south of the old town of Dubrovnik, and it was engaged by naval gunfire, either 57 millimetre or 76 millimetre cannon.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have the map in front of the witness. That's the Exhibit 326, tab 24, the -- and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid my monitor is -- I've touched a button.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please point out the Hotel Excelsior. On the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Given your military background and expertise, could you comment on the accuracy and the effectiveness of this weapon that you've just described?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: The weapon would be regarded as a very accurate weapon. It should have been able to hit a target with some precision. And I was in the Hotel Argentina and was able to observe the shelling of the area of the Hotel Excelsior. I have no doubt that that was the intended target of the naval gunfire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the hotel at that time a military target? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: Not that I was aware of. There was no apparent military presence there at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to the ground forces that you saw active, what weapons did they use, and could you see from where they fired?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I couldn't see from where they fired because they were indirect fire weapons that were being used. They consisted of both mortars and guns, artillery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you comment on the accuracy of such weapons?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: The artillery gun is a relatively accurate weapon. The mortar is less so. But it is all very dependent on a number of factors, including very much the training of the teams, the crews that are handling the guns, the fire control directors, and indeed the meteorological conditions at any particular time?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have now the map 326, tab 13 in front of the witness. It's the wider map of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for clarification for the record, the map we just used is tab 23, not tab 24.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see which regions were targeted by the land forces? What did you see? And please look at the ELMO. And could you tell us -- point out and tell us what it is they targeted.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: This area here is the area of a yachting marina that lay to the north-east of the old town of Dubrovnik. That area was particularly heavily engaged by mortar fire and caused extensive damage to both a large number of very fine yachts and the buildings that were in the marina area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this region -- would you describe -- would you say this was a military target or a civilian target?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I saw nothing of military value within the marina area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they also hit other regions at the time?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: Yes. You would appreciate that it is at some time removed now, and my -- there was quite a lot of shelling going on at the time, so I can indicate the areas in which there was shelling ran along the area from the marina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: In that area there, but also on Mount Srdj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And were there any military targets that were hit or -- yes?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: The only overt military target that I observed was, in fact, Mount Srdj. There was an old Napoleonic fort there that was occupied by armed Croats and there was a communications mast also on that height. Otherwise, the area that I indicated between the marina and south of the town of Dubrovnik, as far as I could see, was occupied only by civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those shells that landed in the civilian regions, could that have been accidentally?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why don't you think that?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I think that the distance for error and the nature, the intensity of the bombardments would indicate that, even allowing for a lot of mistakes by the crews that were serving the weapons, I don't think they were accidental fall of shot on the civilian area, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. The maps can be turned away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Court very briefly and in general terms the degree of preplanning, coordination, and command and control of troops in a joint operation of land and navy forces.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: For a combined forces operation of land, sea, and air, there has to be control and coordination by the commander of the operation, and to do that, he has a coordination or a fire direction centre under his command to coordinate the various fires. And they would plan the resources that would be allocated to any particular target for engagement and the fires that would be available to the elements on the ground. It would take good coordination to mount a joint services operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your information, who was the -- this overall commander?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I was informed that it was General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know his exact position at that time -- rank -- rank and function?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: We were informed that General Strugar was the operational -- the commander of the Operational Group, and he had also been the regional Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. commander in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain how the selection of targets is made in such operations, in particular given the fact that there was residential areas and even a cultural monument.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: Well, the first factor that would be taken into consideration would be the achievement of the mission, the most effective targets to be hit to achieve the mission. The second factor taken into consideration would be the safety and security of one's own forces. And the other factor then of the -- both heritage or civilian areas and heritage. They would also be taken in after the other two factors had been considered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what you saw happening, could you -- could you conclude what the mission was that was to be achieved?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: It wasn't apparent what the mission at that particular time was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already mentioned the fire plan, that is preplanned. Are there also situations when during an attack there are impromptu targets, and can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: Yes. Obviously you can't cater for everything in preplanning, so the fires that take place before the start of an operation can all be preplanned, but once your operation starts, targets will appear that will threaten the accomplishment of your mission or endanger the safety of your own troops and those targets will then be engaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have already mentioned that the overall commander, in this case here Strugar, would be involved in the preplanning. What about the impromptu targets? Who would make these decisions?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: The decisions for impromptu targets could be made at a lower level from the unit or formation that's under threat, but it would be coordinated and the headquarters would be informed about the actions taken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what you personally observed in Dubrovnik, would that indicate a preplanned fire plan or impromptu actions or targets?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I would not be in a position to say whether it was preplanned or impromptu, but I would tend to the view that they were preplanned fires at that particular stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why would you think that?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: Because the -- there was nothing occurring that would direct impromptu fire there. Obviously the shelling was -- to us, it was obvious it was taking place against targets that had been there for quite some time and nothing new had arisen that would cause them to be engaged in an impromptu fashion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have mentioned that the preplanning would be on a level of Strugar. Would the planning of the attack on Dubrovnik that you saw also involve the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I would be surprised if it did not, that such operations had not been coordinated with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would -- while these operations were ongoing, would the ground troops be in constant contact with the overall commander, and would the overall commander be in contact with General Staff, according to experience that you have?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I would imagine so. I would be surprised if they were not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The navy involved in the action, even with impromptu targets, would they coordinate with the land forces?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: In an operation like that, I would imagine that they would have to coordinate with the land forces, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to put to the witness the Exhibit -- tab 2 of Exhibit 400. Tab 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I would like you to look at page 2 on this paragraph on Dubrovnik, and it says here: "In Dubrovnik, our team also reported heavy bombardment during the evening. JNA/Serbian forces appear so far to be sparing the old town, but the naval and mortar attacks launched were aimed at the civilian population. There were no military targets in the area." Would that have been your observation at that time?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: Yes. That report was compiled on foot of reports that we were making from Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the same page, under the headline "Beyond Zagreb," paragraph 3, there is a reference to -- in the middle of this paragraph is a reference to what happened in Karlovac, and there is mentioned: "JNA-backed Serbian irregular forces." Were you aware of such forces?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: If you mean was I aware of such forces in the Karlovac area at that time, I have to remind you that I was in Dubrovnik, and I was not aware of any such forces in the Dubrovnik area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you dealt with Osijek, were you aware of any such irregular forces there?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: At an earlier time in Osijek, I was aware of some irregular forces in that area, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you know who commanded them?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: No, I would not know who commanded them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would now like to put to the witness tab 4 of the Exhibit 400, and it's another report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the first page, the last paragraph, it says here: "I should like you to be aware that those indiscriminate attacks continue despite statements to the contrary by the Serbian and federal authorities." Can you explain this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: That particular paragraph refers to statements that Dubrovnik was not being engaged, and that was issued by the headquarters in Zagreb, but I was present in Dubrovnik on Sunday, the 6th of October, and was a witness, as were the other members of my team, to the attack on the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "issued by the headquarters in Zagreb," which headquarters do you mean?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I mean the headquarters of the EC Monitoring Mission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know with whom they were in contact? Because it says here "... statements to the contrary by the Serbian and federal authorities."

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: They had contact with an Admiral Brovet in Belgrade. I think he had been assigned as the liaison or contact person for the ECMM by the federal authorities, but I know that that was the point of contact in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on page 2 of this same report, there is a reference to the population. It says here: "Meanwhile, the population bolstered by an influx of refugees faces not only shortages of water and electricity but also a deliberate campaign of intimidation." And then there comes some details. Was that actually what you found at the time?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: Yes. There was a large number of refugees in Dubrovnik or in the Lapad area of Dubrovnik. They had been accommodated in hotels, and we visited them and we got firsthand accounts from them of the leaving of their homes, they had been driven out of their homes, and destruction and looting that was going on in the homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And here is mentioning of a deliberate campaign of intimidation. Was that your position, your finding at that time?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: The type of treatment to which the people were subjected to would lead me to believe, yes, that they were being intimidated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. That should be enough for this report. While you were in Dubrovnik, did you see hits in the old town?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: You appreciate that it's quite some time ago now, but to the best of my knowledge and memory, I, at maximum, saw two hits in the old town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you think -- according to what you observed, would you say these were deliberate targeting the old town or more overshots or mistakes?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I would be very much of the opinion that they were wayward shells, that the old town was deliberately -- was not targeted. Because there was so much shelling going on in other areas that it was apparent that the old town at this stage was not being targeted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that the old town was targeted in November, mid-November and on the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: At that stage, I was working in the headquarters of the EC Monitoring Mission in Zagreb, and I was aware that Dubrovnik was targeted. I'm talking of the old town of Dubrovnik was targeted at that particular time, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you actually see a video or -- a video showing the December shelling?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: Not at that time but at some remove later I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what you saw happening there, would that suggest to you that it was preplanning or a, let's say, a spontaneous activity on the 6th? I'm particularly referring to the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I would imagine by the level of activity and the intensity of the fire that there was a level of preplanning had gone into it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to give an idea, preplanning at that level and at that time, what kind of a time frame would the preplanning take? Just an hour, or more, or days? Could you say?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: It would certainly have taken a lot more than an hour. It would have taken 24 hours, 48 hours. I couldn't put an exact time limit, but I -- the planning of a major operation like that would take quite some time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were in Dubrovnik, did you have free and uncontrolled access to parts of the city not controlled by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you meet members of a Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: Yes. We met the chairman of the Crisis Staff and also the mayor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this a civilian Crisis Staff or a military body?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: No, it was a civilian Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was their stage of organisation?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: It was chaotic, I think would be the best way of describing it. They were extremely shaken by the events that were taking place in Dubrovnik. They were certainly traumatised by the situation they found themselves in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see armed personnel in Dubrovnik, and could you estimate the number?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: In the entire Dubrovnik region, I would not be able to estimate a number. In the old city, I saw, at most, ten to 15 armed Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would the -- yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: But outside of that, at various occasions I did see armed Croats in Mount Srdj and in other areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these --

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: But not many. I saw very few.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these professional soldiers to what you saw?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: No, mostly not. I did see a number of the National Guard but not many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe the uniforms, weapons that you saw on these armed Croats.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: The uniforms on the small number of National Guard that I saw were of the disruptive pattern material type, DPM. I then saw police uniforms, and the rest were civilians. With regard to armament, it was all light weaponry; sniper rifles, assault rifles. The heaviest weapon I saw with any one person was a RPG-7. That is a hand-held anti-tank rocket. And the only other weapon I saw was an armoured car with a light machine-gun in the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Beginning October at the time when you were there, was there any effective defence in Dubrovnik? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: No. There was no defence put in place in any way. I could not describe Dubrovnik as a defended city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the JNA know that, do you know?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I'm not party to what the JNA knew or did not know, but I would be very surprised if they did not know the state of the defences, because they had direct observation onto the area from the naval forces that they had deployed offshore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were in Dubrovnik, did you observe any Croatian positions or preparations for positions in the old town or near the old town?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any such positions or preparations for positions in the refugee hotels that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the armed men that you saw in the old town. Were they present there in any offensive or defensive role? Could you see that?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: No. They were not in any describable military role. The numbers I saw appeared to be exhausted, they appeared to be traumatised by events that took place in other areas, and certainly were in no fit condition to fight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anything that -- did you see the Croats provoking the shelling of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the JNA under threat through the weapons that the Croats had?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: Not under any threat or major threat that I could see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any military advantage that the JNA could gain by their attack on Dubrovnik that you could see?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: No. I could not see that there was any great military advantage to be gained by taking the city of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were in Dubrovnik, did you also try to reach the JNA to solve the situation through negotiations?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: Our main mission in going to Dubrovnik was in fact to try and effect a cease-fire in the area, and we made numerous attempts to contact the JNA authorities. I should say that before we went to Dubrovnik, we had been given the name of the commander, General Strugar, and we had been given a telephone number, or telephone numbers, to contact his headquarters. So when we were in Dubrovnik, during the time we were there we made numerous attempts to contact the JNA by telephone. All of those attempts were in vain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it because there was no connection did you actually get a connection?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I had a member of my team who was a Serbo-Croat speaker, a Dane Lars Boland. He made contact on a number of occasions and got somebody on the other end of the line, and as soon as they heard that we belonged to the ECMM, the phone went dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you form an opinion about the JNA's willingness to negotiate?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: It was obvious that they didn't want to have any contact with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: The Croatian authorities at this stage, as I have described, were in a very bad and excitable situation and were desperate to achieve a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the Belgrade or Zagreb level? Any negotiations there at that time, and between whom?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: We were in contact with Zagreb, our headquarters in Zagreb, by telephone, and we were describing the events in Dubrovnik, and we were assured that efforts were being made to get the assault stopped at the level of the headquarters. I understood that the headquarters were in contact with the authorities in Belgrade, and I understood that it was Admiral Brovet that they were in contact with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were complaints from the ECMM lodged against what was happening?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: We were assured by our headquarters that protests were lodged about the matters that were taking place in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To whom were these protests addressed? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I was told that they were addressed to the authorities in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The military authorities?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the political authorities? Do you know whether complaints were lodged with them?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: No. The contacts, as I said, were with the General Staff contact, Admiral Brovet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were the reactions on those protests? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: There appeared to be little or no reaction to them that I could perceive from my position on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to put to the witness tab 6 of Exhibit 400. And it is a report again, and it's from the 10th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I would like to direct you to page 2, the paragraph 5, and it says here: "A bombardment directed from JNA positions around Cavtat and Plat ceased within an hour of notification to Belgrade, indicating that the news of the cease-fire may not have reached the units concerned." Can you comment on this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: Well, the -- the hour delay would be indicative of the time lag for the instructions to filter down from Belgrade to the units on the ground, because that is not an instantaneous thing, it takes time to happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And given your experience, does that indicate anything in relation to command and control?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: Well, it would indicate that the units that were fighting in the Dubrovnik area were in the command chain from the General Staff in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And now I would like to put to the witness tab 8 of Exhibit 400.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in relation -- on page 2, there are several paragraphs relating to Dalmatia, referring to discussions about -- or even cease-fires, in relation to deblocking barracks and cease-fires along the coastline. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in paragraph 11 of that document, there is a reference to cease-fire violations, and it says here -- it gives here two choices: "There could be a selective minimum associated with regrouping, or equally the product of an imperfect control of local JNA and irregular units." Could you please explain this.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: That is somebody in the report offering a reason for the breaches that may have occurred within that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it is here the Vukovar area. Did you observe anything or did you get information on anything happening to this effect in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: At this particular time, I was not in Dubrovnik, but I was aware that the Dubrovnik area was part of the wider cease-fire, and that had taken place within that area. Our successor team, I was aware that they had made contact and had effected a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Summarising what you saw happening in Dubrovnik while you were there and also what you heard afterwards, would you call this a battle between two opposing forces?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: No, I would not call it a battle between two opposing forces. As I have said earlier, I saw very little evidence of Croatian armament or preparation for actions and, consequently, it could not have been said to be a battle between two forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are the questions of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A preliminary question first, General. Most or almost all of your testimony relates to Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you came here, did you come to testify with the conviction or any knowledge that the Republic of Serbia had any connection -- the Republic of Serbia and I personally, for instance, had anything to do with those events around Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I did not have a conviction or evidence that you personally were connected with the events in Dubrovnik. I have evidence of what I saw within Dubrovnik and the factors that indicated to me that what was taking place in Dubrovnik was taking place with the control of the General Staff headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am not speaking only about me, because I hope that is not in dispute, me personally, but I'm asking about the Republic of Serbia. Did you come to know that the Republic of Serbia had any role in the events that you have described?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: The forces that were engaged in the Dubrovnik area were the forces of the JNA, as far as I was aware.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you present during any meeting between representatives of the authorities of Dubrovnik and representatives of JNA command staff in the area?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: No, I was not. As I said, we made strenuous efforts on numerous occasions to make contact with them, to no avail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but you probably know that there were a number of such meetings that have been testified about by witnesses sitting in the same seat that you're occupying now and who had attended those meetings, and they were held almost or most frequently in the presence of representatives of the international community. Do you know anything about those meetings?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I know that subsequent to my time in Dubrovnik, the team that succeeded us conducted meetings in the Cavtat area with the JNA and the Croatian authorities, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you have any information gained from documents, because you were not there, the same way that I learn about these things from documents, that the main demand of the JNA, the main and only request was for the armed formations, irregulars -- irregular armed formations to leave Dubrovnik and that they did not make any other demands?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I'm aware that those demands were made, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I find something rather strange or illogical. A moment ago you were saying that there was some sort of intention - and I really hear this for the first time - on the part of the JNA to depopulate Dubrovnik, whereas at meetings held between the JNA and representatives of Dubrovnik, there is exclusive emphasis on the demand for armed groups to leave Dubrovnik with their weapons and along secure routes where they would not be exposed to any danger. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I am aware that that took place subsequent to my time in Dubrovnik. The events that I spoke about were from the 5th of October to the 7th of October, and at that time, there were no -- there was no significant armed presence of Croats within the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you consider to be "significant armed presence"? You said that "there was no significant armed presence." Why would there be any military presence in Dubrovnik, which was a demilitarised town for Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. decades?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There are two questions there. The first question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Significant armed presence, if I could take that. A significant armed presence would be a coherent, directed, and armed with, I would suggest, more than assault rifles and light weapons. I would have expected to have heavier weaponry in a coherent force that would present a threat to the very considerable force of the JNA within the area. The second question: Why should there be an armed presence within the area at all? Well, the light arms that I saw were certainly not a significant armed presence, and why they should be there at all, the reports we had received, which initially I said we were disinclined to believe, about the city of Dubrovnik becoming under threat turned out to be very real indeed. So I would have thought that there would have been some necessity for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, General. Let us try and be efficient and cover the matters you have testified about. In July 1991, you were based in Zagreb. This was a monitoring mission of the European Community in those days to prevent the crisis, as the wording was in those days.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who are the signatories of the memorandum on the presence of the monitoring mission of the European Community? It was signed on the 13th of July, 1991, and it served as the basis for your presence there.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I am afraid at this remove I don't remember who the signatories of that document were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me remind you. Representatives of the Federal Ministry for Foreign Affairs of Yugoslavia, Slovenia, and Croatia. And on behalf of the European Community, an ambassador in the Foreign Ministry of the Netherlands because, as you quite correctly noted, the Netherlands at the time was chairing the European Community, and the name of the Ambassador was Christiaan Kroner. Do you now remember?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I don't remember that ambassador as being the head of mission of the EC monitor mission. In July 1991, Van der Valk [phoen] was the head of mission. He subsequently handed over, in September, to Van Houten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the signatories on the memorandum and not who headed the mission. Tell me, please, very briefly with a yes or no, were you familiar with the contents of the memorandum of the mission of which you were a senior official in those days?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: At this remove, I'm not familiar with the memorandum you mention, but I certainly would have been at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that the main mandate of the monitoring mission was, A, to assist in stabilising the cease-fire within which the blockade of units and facilities of the JNA would be lifted; and B, to oversee the suspension of the declarations on independence for three months, as agreed on by Yugoslavia, Slovenia and Croatia, the parties hosting the missions. Do you recollect that? Is that what is stated in the memorandum?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: Perhaps not in those exact words, but that was the sense of the memorandum, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if you're going to quote from the document and you want to rely on it and ask the witness questions about it, the fairest thing is to put the document to him. Now, have you got it in English so that we can all see it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have it, Mr. May. But if the witness believes that I didn't quote from it correctly, he can simply say that he doesn't remember or that it is not right so that I am not in any way trying to mislead him in his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying you are trying to mislead him, but for the efficient conduct of the case, if this is a document of importance, we should have it. Perhaps the Prosecution can assist us, in due course, if they've got a copy of it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that the opposing side can gain possession of that document, because it must exist in their archives and in the archives of Yugoslavia, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the 13th of July, 1991, when the memorandum was signed, the mission's task was to assist in stabilising the cease-fire within the framework of which the lifting of the blockade would take place of the units and facilities of the JNA, which only confirms that those facilities and units were already under blockade at that time. And secondly, which is extremely important from the political standpoint, to supervise the suspension of the implementation of the independence declarations for three months, as the parties had agreed. The federal government of Yugoslavia had agreed on this with the leaderships of Croatia and Slovenia. Is that right, General?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember, General -- I'm just asking: Do you remember that that memorandum should have ensured the consistent implementation of the so-called Brioni declaration which, on the 7th of July, 1991, which means only a few days prior to that, had been issued in the presence of the ministerial troika of the European Community? Again, it was in the presence of the federal authorities and representatives of Slovenia and Croatia. And then this was followed as a consequence of that declaration by this memorandum. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I don't remember the -- I remember the Brioni agreement, the issuing of it. In what presence it took place, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Without any doubt this can be found in documents, so I won't insist on it, but do you recollect, as you say you know of the Brioni declaration, that Slovenia and Croatia had pledged through that declaration that they would deblock all units and facilities of the JNA and restore the former regime on the frontier of SFRY within a period of 24 hours? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I cannot remember all the detail of it, but I do remember that certain undertakings were made with respect to the blockades, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct to say that representatives of Slovenia and Croatia undertook specifically to refrain from any unilateral acts of violence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You know, it would be much simpler if we just had the document rather than asking the witness for a memory test. The chances of remembering this kind of detail is small. We'll get both these documents, please. Just a moment. We'll get both these documents. If the Prosecution would get them during the break, please. I think we've had the Brioni declaration. I have a recollection we've got that exhibited, but I may be wrong. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Brioni declaration is one thing, and then came a second document, the memorandum on the presence of the monitoring mission of the European Community, dated the 13th of July, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll get both.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want to fatigue you, General, with questions regarding general political matters. On page 1 of your statement, and I quote, you said that you were first sent to Slovenia to monitor the safe withdrawal of the JNA from Slovenia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: Among other duties that we had there, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that what was involved was the relocation of the commands and units of the JNA from Slovenia to other parts of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on the basis of a decision of the Presidency of the SFRY taken on the 18th of July, 1991?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that, and we witnessed the withdrawal of the JNA units from Slovenia to other parts of the Federal Republic, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have in your hands this decision of the Presidency? I'm asking you this because the decision was taken to relocate them outside of Slovenia, but that that would not preempt the future regulation of relations in Yugoslavia nor would it call in question its territorial integrity. Did you have access to that Presidency decision, the consequences of which you were monitoring?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I don't remember that we had access to that Presidency decision at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you did not, do you remember that after that decision and after the decision started to be implemented, that in spite of this goodwill shown, that both in the Republic of Slovenia and the Republic of Croatia, a series of attacks were launched against JNA units?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: No, that's not my memory, particularly in respect of Slovenia. The situation in Croatia was a lot more complicated than that, but again, I am not mindful of any attack that took place in Slovenia after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you are not aware of it, I will not ask you any more questions about it. Did you ever receive any information as to the number of attacks made by the police and the Territorial Defence of Slovenia against officers, soldiers, and JNA convoys during those activities, including their mistreatment, harassment, and where these incidents took place? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I have to be very clear on this one at this stage. There were reports of conflict between convoys and police and armed elements in Slovenia prior to our arrival in the area, which would have been at the end of June 1991 and early July, perhaps. But from the end of the -- from the implementation of the Brioni agreement and our arrival in the area, there were no reports and no evidence was offered to us of any conflict between the Slovenians and the JNA subsequent to that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, just that the Brioni declaration was just mentioned. It is Exhibit 330, tab 35. But it is only marked for identification. It was actually part of the binder from President Mesic, and it's only marked for identification, and maybe this is the possibility to now actually tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us deal with that after the adjournment. We will find it, and we can deal with it. And if you would get us, if you can, the 13th of July memorandum, if you can get that up during the break. We will come back to it afterwards. Thank you. I've just been handed a copy. It might be convenient to exhibit it. We will exhibit the Brioni declaration separately now. I will ask that copies be made and it will take the next Defence exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Defence Exhibit 104, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can I hand it back. Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you're saying that there were no attacks after this document and signature of representatives of Slovenia and Croatia together with representatives of the federal authorities, are you aware and there is any report of your mission about Croatian paramilitary units, the National Guards Corps, on the 29th of August - so you see yourself how much later this was - attacked a railway column, 29 freight trucks in the village of Ivankovo when the escort was disarmed and JNA property looted. This was during the process of dislocating this development from Slovenia and on the railroad, a part of the railroad running from Zagreb to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, we are moving from the witness's evidence. Since he was present, I take it, in Croatia at the time he can answer it, but it may be he's got no particular knowledge of this matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I emphasise one thing? When I said that there were no attacks or fighting between the JNA and the Slovenians, I meant exactly that in the territory of the Republic of Slovenia. What the defendant has just referred to took place on Croatian territory, and I would have to refresh my memory on the reports with regard to that particular incident. I don't remember it. But it's -- I'm not -- I am not ruling it out. What I'd specifically said was that there were no attacks within the Slovenian area. That's what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the memorandum that followed the Brioni declaration and that was signed by the authorities of the Slovenia, Croatia, and the federal authorities. So it is one whole. Tell me, do you recollect that armed members --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Mr. Milosevic, you specifically asked the witness about Slovenia, and he's answered. Now you want to move on to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked him this happened in Croatia, but I had in mind that the general was a senior officer in the monitoring mission of the European Community in Zagreb, and that's why I'm asking him this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that armed members, or do you remember that armed National Guards Corps members on that same day and the next day again, on the 30th of August, in the village of Mirkovci, again looted JNA property, seizing quartermaster supplies and other supplies? Do you remember that incident?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I don't remember that specific incident. I would have to refresh my memory on any reports we had on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that the mandate of the monitoring mission of the European Community was reinforced and expanded on the 2nd of September, 1991, with a memorandum on the monitoring mission?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: The precise date I don't remember, but it was in September, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in principle, since you probably cannot give me a very concrete answer, but as concretely as you can, within the context of your monitoring of what you said the safe withdrawal of the JNA from Slovenia and Croatia, in view of these attacks on JNA property, tell me, please, the monitoring mission of the European Community, in your opinion - and I'm asking you for your opinion - did it successfully fulfil its mandate of the 13th of July, 1991?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: The specific instance you've mentioned, I would have to refresh my memory of them, as I said, from reports at that time. Whether you're asking me in the overall whether the European Monitoring Mission was successful, I would have to say that in the -- with respect to preventing an outbreak of fighting in the area, it certainly didn't succeed in preventing large scale fighting taking place, because as you well know, in November and December, which was much later, there was very heavy fighting throughout the area of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And is it true that you could have assessed and investigated the violation of the agreement about a cease-fire, which was agreed upon on the 1st of September, 1991, in Belgrade? Once again, between the federal authorities.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: The investigation and reporting on the numerous cease-fires that were agreed was the mission of the monitor mission, and they saw reported upon all of the breaches that took place in respect of cease-fires, yes. And the expansion of the mission that you referred to on the 2nd of September would have encompassed that, and the monitor mission became much more active in the area of Croatia after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, then. And is it true and correct that, pursuant to that agreement, and you were duty bound to supervise its implementation, that all the paramilitary and irregular forces and units had to be disarmed and disbanded, including the reserve forces of the Croatian National Guard Corps? And that's what it says in Article 1 of the mentioned memorandum of the 2nd of September, 1991. It is the memorandum concerning your monitoring mission. Do you know that? Do you happen to remember that?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: As I said to you, I can't remember the detail, but I remember that the mission did undertake the supervision of cease-fires within the area and that there were certain conditions attached to it. But this is another document, and I ask that I should have sight of it also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I haven't got it here with me?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I'm sure you will be able to find it in the archives, and could you provide the witness with a copy, please. But the point is, on Article 1 of that same memorandum, where all the paramilitaries and irregular units had to be disarmed and disbanded, including the reserve force of the Croatian National Guard Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've already dealt with this. Again, perhaps we can try and find that memorandum of the cease-fire. Perhaps the Prosecution can assist us with those two documents now. It's time for an adjournment. Mr. Milosevic, you can have another three-quarters of an hour, if you want it, in cross-examination. That will allow for the fact that the witness has given live evidence but also that his statement was admitted. You get extra time for that. General, could you be back, please, in twenty minutes. I must formally remind you not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have located both memoranda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If we could have them, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, they are not exhibited so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll deal with this now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the memorandum will be Defence Exhibit 104, and -- Your Honours, I apologise for that. The memorandum is Defence Exhibit 105, and the memo of the cease-fire, dated 2nd September 1991, is Defence Exhibit 106. Your Honours, Defence Exhibit 106 is titled the Memorandum of Understanding on the Extension of the Monitoring Activities of the Monitor Mission to Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We've now got those documents, Mr. Milosevic. If you want to ask the witness about any of them, then he will need a copy. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I assume that the witness now has a copy of this. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I mentioned a moment ago, General, in Article 1, towards the end of the page, everything else is enumerated before that, and then at the very end of that page, it says: "The Croat National Guard reserve forces shall be demobilised." And so on and so forth. So that's what I was referring to when I asked you about it. So tell me now, please, General, in your statement, on page 2, paragraph 1 of your statement, you say that on one occasion you went to Slavonia with a man named Branko who was a member of the National Guards Corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know at the time that the Croatian National Guard Corps was in fact a paramilitary and illegal armed formation precisely incorporated in this agreement?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: Yes, and there were other forces precisely incorporated in the agreement in the Osijek area at that particular time; the weapons and equipment of the JNA that were operating in the area and irregular forces. That was the reason for our presence there, was trying to negotiate a cease-fire between the two elements so that this agreement could then be properly implemented. That is the reason. That was the purpose of the monitor team that had been sent to Osijek at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know that, with respect to the illegal formation of the Croatian National Guard Corps at the end of June 1991, the federal government of Yugoslavia took steps before the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia calling for the fact that the ZNG as a professional armed formation be characterised as an unconstitutional and unlawful act on the part of the Republic of Croatia? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the detail of that particular legislation, but what I am aware of is that there were a number of armed elements on both sides of the equation during the hostilities in Croatia, and as I said to you, our objective was going there to ensure the carrying out of the agreement and to bring about a cease-fire and peace to the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia, on the 16th of October, 1991, made the decision to proclaim it irregular and unconstitutional, this formation and establishment of the National Guard Corps? Because -- that apart from the armed forces of Yugoslavia, no other armed formations could be set up, as did the Republic of Croatia in placing the National Guard Corps under the command of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia. Are you familiar with that? Just give me a yes or no answer, please.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: As I said to you, I'm not familiar with the precise legislation, but I have to say that there was a number of armed elements operating at that particular time, and our objective was to bring about a stand-down of all in a coordinated and precise manner, which we found, as I have to say, extremely difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that, General. But this question doesn't refer to you yourself personally. What I'm asking you is whether you consider that your mission consistently insisted upon the disarming and disbanding of the ZNG and other paramilitary formations that were established at that time in Croatia, at least with the same intensity that it attended the dynamics of the dislocation of the JNA units from Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I consider that the EC monitor mission carried out their mission in Croatia in as evenhanded a fashion and as just a fashion as they possibly could. I would have no doubt that they did not show fear or favour to either side. But they did stand for the peace-making and for human rights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you say that the JNA forces at that time were exposed to attacks when they were in their bases and barracks in Croatia; is that right? And do you know anything about the number of attacks that were launched, how intense they were, and so on?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: It is not correct to say that I said in my statement that they were exposed to attacks in their barracks and bases in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, were they or not?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: They were on occasions, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, then. Now, did you know about - and I assume that you would have had to have known - about the report by the Federal Secretary for National Defence, General Veljko Kadijevic, dated the 12th of September, 1991, in which it is stated that up until that date, that is to say up until the 12th of September, 1991, or, rather, from the 2nd of September, 1991, ten days, all the barracks and facilities of the JNA were under a complete siege, complete blockade? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
