utterances.text: I was aware of the barracks and facilities being blockaded, yes. I would like to remind the defendant that at this particular time, I was a monitor. I wasn't the executive chief of the EC monitor mission. Very often I was in the field with a monitor team, so consequently, I would not have been aware of the detail of all of the announcements and agreements that possibly were made. But naturally in the spirit and in the carrying out of our mission, I would have been made aware of the contents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that as of the date the agreement was signed, up Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. until the 11th of September, the Croatian forces carried out 115 attacks against members of the JNA and that in the barracks at that time five officers were killed, six soldiers, and 40 members of the JNA wounded? Did you have reports to that effect? So they were in their barracks. They weren't engaged in any other kinds of activities.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: That level of detail with regard to reports, I have no memory of it at this time. I am aware that there were a number of attacks on the barracks that were occupied by the JNA in Croatia at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you do know that there were attacks against barracks and that people were killed and so on. Have I understood you correctly? Was that your answer?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell me, please, what your mission undertook with respect to these flagrant violations of the cease-fire agreement, that is, by the Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: The mission, when there were breaches of the cease-fire agreement on any side, endeavoured to negotiate with the parties and to bring them to the realisation that it was only by cooperation with the mission and the full implementation of the agreement could peace be restored to the situation. So as I said, they operated in an evenhanded fashion to both sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I was asking you, General, about these attacks against soldiers sitting in their barracks. So they weren't in any kind of military operation and activity except that they were in the barracks where they had been for 50 years, in garrisons throughout Yugoslavia. So in your own country, General -- let me ask you this, in view of your experience and your official function: In your own country, attacks on the regular army, the regular army of a sovereign country, in view of the fact that you are well placed to respond to that question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think this is going to be a question which is -- is going to be a matter which we're going to have to decide it may be ultimately. It's not a hypothetical question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, but I'm asking the witness, Mr. May, whether in his own country --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And I'm stopping you. So could you go on to the next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this then, please: Is it correct and true that in the Republic of Ireland there is a law in force against acts of violence and terror which is called Offences Against the Act, and it is the 31st --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is irrelevant what the Republic of Ireland's laws are. What we're concerned with is what happened in Croatia. We'll consider the situation in due course. Now, would you move on to another topic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, as to what happened in Croatia, can these attacks being characterised as acts against the state and crimes against the state and security of the state?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, General, if you think you can answer it, do. It's probably a matter which we're going to have to decide.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I would like to say in that respect, there was a particular situation pertaining at that time in Croatia, and the legitimacy or otherwise of the regime that was in force is a political question which I was not a party to and will not offer an opinion on at this particular time. So consequently, I'm not going to stray into that area. I offered my evidence as to the facts of what I saw when I was there and the manner in which we carried out our mission, and I'll confine myself to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine, then. I won't ask you any more about that. Now, when you talk about your stay in Dubrovnik in the Hotel Argentina during a period of six days, I think you said that several shells fell quite near to your hotel; is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And some witnesses who were here before you said that the forces, the Croatian forces, in fact, had deployed combat positions around that hotel. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: Not at that particular time, they hadn't. During the time I was there, they had not. The hotel in question was the Hotel Excelsior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when you talk about the legitimacy or illegitimacy of military targets in the Dubrovnik area, and you mean the targets hit by the JNA when you say that, are you quite sure that what was hit by the JNA in fact was an illegitimate military target?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: If you wish to describe it as such, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I assume most probably, General, that you know about The Hague rules, about the laws of war and customs of war, 1907, determining the status of an undefended place or town?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, I assume that a place or town, in order to have the status of undefended, it must fulfil the following conditions: That all the fighters, military materiel and movable equipment have been evacuated, that immovable military installations and facilities are not used for hostilities, that the authorities and population do not take any military acts or to support military operations. So those several elements. Let's take them. Are you aware of those elements?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I am aware of that. And when I -- I didn't describe Dubrovnik as and undefended city in the context of The Hague Convention, it having been declared as such. So it was in the context of the verb "to defend," and purely on that basis, on the military basis, that I was dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I assume that you're not challenging the fact that members of the armed forces were located in the town, however you wish to call them or qualify them; regular, irregular, or whatever. From what you yourself say on page 6: Groups of armed people with Kalashnikovs, snipers, hunting rifles, et cetera, that you saw a mortar and that the Croatian National Guard Corps had several mortars in its possession. This is on page 5 of your statement. And so on. So are you challenging that?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: No, not at all. In fact, that is my evidence. The only thing I will challenge is you say that I saw a mortar. I didn't say I saw a mortar. I said I heard them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You heard it, which means that fire was opened against the JNA. Are you challenging that?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: No. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know how many members of the JNA were killed in the Dubrovnik region from that fire, from the shooting?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, as you're a professional soldier yourself and occupy the top positions in your army today, if I tell you that 152 soldiers lost their lives in the Dubrovnik region, fired on and shot at by the Croatian sides, do you consider that this shooting could be characterised in some kind of non-intensive shooting or - how shall I put this? - weak fire or anything of that kind?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I would like clarification of the period in which the 152 soldiers lost their lives, because as I said, I was there from the 5th to the 7th of October inclusive. So was it during that period 152 soldiers lost their lives? Is that what you're telling me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, not during the time that you were there. I wasn't claiming that, General. I'm just asking about this figure, whether you know about this figure of persons killed in the area.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: No, I do not know that that was the figure. And certainly the amount of fire that I observed from the Croatian side would be -- would not indicate to me that any number of casualties of that nature were inflicted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned, General, a moment ago during the examination-in-chief, the fact that you had received information to the effect that Dubrovnik was in danger, and your comments were that you considered this information to be unfounded. When did you receive that piece of information? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: The precise date I couldn't say, but it would have been towards the end of September 1991, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you receive similar information and compare it with the information that your team received, which was in Dubrovnik at that time? I think the code name was the Whisky team, I think, as yours was Charlie. The Whisky dispatch and yours was Charlie, I believe.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I think I'd better clarify something in that respect. The Team Whisky was dispatched to Dubrovnik as a result of those reports we had received, to confirm them or otherwise. That's the reason why they went to Dubrovnik at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But you received that information from the Croatian side; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could we then conclude that giving out this kind of information was in fact preparation for a future provocation against the JNA by the armed forces concentrated around Dubrovnik at that time?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't conclude that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you mentioned that the reports in Zagreb were written by people who were actually sitting in Zagreb and were not in the field on the ground. Isn't that right, or have I misunderstood you?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: The reports were sent by monitors in the field to the headquarters, and the reports that were subsequently sent to The Hague from Zagreb were constructed by people operating in the headquarters. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, General, just in a few words if possible, why did you give up this RMCM01 exhibit that Mr. Kay mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness explained it had nothing to do with him. It was somebody else's observations. So he can't produce it. That's what he explained.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you spoke about the JNA. Tell me, why when you're referring to the JNA in your statement and the attachment which is number RMCM02 of the 6th of December, 1991, why do you equate it with the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you like to have the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to see the document, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Find the attachment and the tab number. Can you say what it is, please, for the record. Mr. Milosevic, let's find this document so we can make sure we have it. It's -- you've mentioned the 6th of December. Do you mean the 6th of October for the numbered attachment?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 6th of October, that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's our Exhibit 400, attachment 2. And you can remind us what it is you put to the witness. Mr. Milosevic, where is it Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in the document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't got it in front of me just now, but he equates the JNA with Serb forces. That's how he refers to them and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- conceives of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's find the passage that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Paragraph 7, which is the second page, in the bottom paragraph there. "JNA/Serbian forces."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you equate that, take that to be the same thing, General?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: That is a report that was submitted at that time from Zagreb to The Hague. That was the manner in which it was written. I -- it was a perception at that particular time that on -- and I say it from a point of simplicity, that there were Serbs and Croats in conflict with each other. But strictly speaking, and the point is that as far as we were concerned, at that time those of us who were in Dubrovnik, it was the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So not Serb forces but the JNA; right?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: That's my understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know the multinational structure of the JNA? Are you aware of that, even at that time, particularly the officers, officer cadre of the JNA, that they were multi-ethnic?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned, General, the fact that there were certain protests against the monitoring mission because of its activities in the Dubrovnik region, and you said there were no reactions to the protests by the army. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: At our time there, you understood me correctly that the protests were made by our mission headquarters in Zagreb. It didn't bring about a reaction on the ground, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if that's so, General, would you please comment on the following -- this is also a document that I received from the other side over there, Mr. May, and it is 00544945, page -- that's the page. And it is a letter by the Deputy Federal Secretary for National Defence, Admiral Stane Brovet, to the head of the monitoring mission, Ambassador GDY Horten [phoen] in Belgrade. The 6th of November is the date. And in that letter, among others, he says: "With respect to the protests of the monitoring mission of the European Community for the activities in the Dubrovnik region on the 2nd and 3rd of November, we have collected information from which the following emerges." And now I would like to ask you whether you were aware of that information and facts. First, it says here, and I'm sure you know, General, that Admiral Brovet was the Deputy Federal National Defence Secretary, a Slovene by ethnicity. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I am, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And first of all, it says: "On the 2nd of November, 1991, from 1300 to 1420 hours, the JNA positions in the Glogov-Kamen region, sniper and mortar fire was opened on them from the Babin Kuk position, Mala Petka [phoen], Lapad and the Nunziata fort [phoen]. And from the same positions, opened fire between 15 and 1620 hours, from guns -- 85 millimetre guns and mortars of 82 and 102 millimetres -- 120 millimetres. And the deployment of the fighter units, groups of six, members of the Croatian National Guard Corps, a diversionary group, infiltrated into their ranks; and it says that on the 2nd of November, all the JNA units were ordered to cease fire at once because in agreement with the EEC monitors work was started to set the Komuvac [phoen] transformer station into operation and the Crisis Staff of Dubrovnik was informed of this as was the EC mission with the violations of the cease-fire agreement. As the attacks did not cease but, on the contrary, were intensified, about 1730 hours mortar fire and machine-gun fire was opened from the positions from which the Croatian armed formations were active. And this is what the letter to the head of your mission, Ambassador Van Houten contains. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the detail in that letter. As I said, my period in the Dubrovnik area was not at the period that you're referring to there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am speaking about a response to protests because the JNA had opened fire, and Admiral Brovet, in his letter, explains the attacks that came prior to this response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has said that he's not familiar with the detail. He wasn't there at the period. Now, you can put it to other witnesses or you can give evidence about it, but there's no point asking the witness about something which he knows nothing of. It just takes up time unnecessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, is it clear that at an adequate level of responsibility held by Admiral Brovet provided an adequate answer as to why fire had to be returned against positions from which it had been opened against the JNA?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: On that particular occasion, it would be -- appear to be the response of Admiral Brovet. That is quite correct, in respect of that particular incident of which I said I have no knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you familiar with the letter of the Federal Secretary for National Defence, General Veljko Kadijevic, addressed to the chairman of the ministerial council of the European Community, Hans van den Broek and the head of the monitoring mission, Ambassador van Houten, in which he says - and this was dated the 6th of November, too - that on the 10th of November, the conclusions of the government of the Republic of Croatia come into effect, and after that date, members of the JNA in the territory of Croatia would be treated as members of an occupying hostile army and clearly Croatia wishes a further escalation of the conflict with unforeseeable consequences. This is corroborated by the fact that Croatian forces bombed certain areas in the Republic of Serbia, including the town of Apotin. Are you familiar with the contents of that letter?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the contents of that letter, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you familiar --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If this is another November letter, I think it's just wasting time. Now, your time is going on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. I have quite a number of documents here which I consider to be important to clear up this matter. I too would like to clear it up. But let me move on then. I will not refer to further documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 6, General, you analyse the justification of the entry of the JNA into the Dubrovnik harbour. You even link this to other naval bases on the Adriatic as part of the protection of the integrity of the SFRY. So my question really is: Why would the regular army, on its own territory in this case, a part of that army that is called the Navy, should not use its own harbours and coastline, and on what basis are you saying that the Dubrovnik harbour had no military, strategic or economic significance for the JNA?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I didn't say that it had no economic significance for the JNA, but what I was saying there is that they were not using Dubrovnik harbour at that time, and they had a number of other bases in the Adriatic. So I couldn't see that they needed to take on a new base in Dubrovnik. That was the case I was making.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is the point, General, when you talk about taking. Don't you think it is extremely illogical for the army to take the territory of its own state? You also mention capitulation, that its own population should capitulate. What logic can there be in this or what explanation can be given for this?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: That logic would be to ignore the factual situation that was taking place on the ground, and that was that there was a state of confrontation between the army that you mentioned and the population within Croatia. Consequently, that was the situation that we were trying to normalise and which we were trying to pacify. That was the whole purpose of us being there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but, General, the behaviour of the JNA which held positions on the fringes of the town and which never entered the town, doesn't that confirm the statement of the JNA leadership that the army had no intention of taking Dubrovnik? But it was the media manipulations and provocations that turned this into a political event which was construed on the basis of those provocations in order to speed up international support for something absurd, as an attack on a tourist centre and a historical monument would be. That was certainly not the intention of the army.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I was at a loss to interpret the intentions of the army at that particular time, but I was aware that while I was there, whereas the old city hadn't been shelled, the areas around it inhabited by the civilians had been, and it was in that context that I was talking of the attack on Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I find something illogical there. You use the explanation that the probable intention was to depopulate Dubrovnik. On page 2 -- no, not of your statement. But on the other hand, you also mentioned Ilok, which was not attacked at all but was evacuated. I assume because it was close to the area of conflict. It was not destroyed or damaged in any sense, but it was evacuated by the Croatian authorities and the Croatian mayor. Why was it evacuated? You even say that international monitors assisted in that evacuation. Why was that town evacuated when no one was attacking it? And here you say that it was attacked for the population to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Information that we had in respect of Ilok was that the people felt increasingly threatened in the town of Ilok, and they asked that they would be evacuated. It struck me as strange that people would be asked to be evacuated from their town unless they were under some threat. So it is not illogical to say that the attack on the population of Dubrovnik would bring about an evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But didn't you know that at meetings held by the authorities of Dubrovnik with JNA representatives in the presence of international representatives, the only demand of the army was for the armed formations, the irregulars, foreign mercenaries leave Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've already been over this ground and the witness has answered that he was not involved in any of these negotiations, although he'd heard of that demand. No point going over that ground again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But that demand, as far as I understood the witness, the witness said that he knew about it, the demand for the armed formations to leave the town, Mr. May, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Now, what new do you want to ask? You've got about five minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will finish in five minutes, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, General, that when you were in the old town of Dubrovnik you saw only two minor damages and that your professional judgement was that these had occurred incidentally.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Allegations here are being repeatedly made that the army wanted to capture Dubrovnik, and Dubrovnik was not captured. Allegations are being presented that the army wanted to destroy Dubrovnik, and Dubrovnik was not destroyed. Is that so or not, General?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not for the general to comment on allegations such as that, which in my recollection have not been made. I think that's your misrepresentation. Now, move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, do you know that Croatian paramilitary forces - and your mission was informed about this - opened fire in the area of Dubrovecki Glebane [phoen] from a vessel against a vessel of the Yugoslav navy? Did you have any report of that? This, for instance, occurred on the 11th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: At this remove, I can't remember that particular incident as I wasn't in that area. On the 11th of November, I was probably back in Zagreb. But I can't remember that incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that fire was constantly opened against JNA units in the villages of Bosanka, Kriza, Bogeja [phoen] and Knezica? Did you have such a report? Did you have access to that information?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: We had information that -- of fire being directed by one side against the other throughout a number -- a large number of locations within Croatia. I don't remember those precise locations on that particular date. I think that there -- only those who were there at that the time or those who would have made the exact report on it could be expected to remember the detail of every incident that took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you now use the expression "one side firing against the other." Can we infer from that that there was a constant exchange of fires between the two sides there, in your professional judgement?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I wouldn't use the word "constant," but there were outbreaks of fighting quite frequently throughout November and December at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're saying that there were outbreaks of fighting throughout November and December, which means fire was opened by both sides. There was a battle going on between two sides. Is that right, General?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in those battles members of the Croatian military or, rather, paramilitary forces were also opening fire from positions within the old town? I have here a bulletin of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence dated the 12th of November, 1991, where this is stated. I have no other sources of information, but I assume that this is correct. Are you familiar with that? That is that fire was opened also from positions within the old town.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: That is dated the 12th of November. I have no knowledge of fire being opened from within the town on that date. But let me clarify something. Can we go back to the question and the answer I gave. "... there were outbreaks of fighting throughout November and December, which means fire was opened by both sides. There was a battle between two sides. Is that right, General?" That question. I said, "That is correct," but my understanding of your question was throughout the Federal Republic of Croatia, on Croatian territory, not within the Dubrovnik area, and my answer was made accordingly. Now you're specifically saying on the 12th of December -- or I beg your pardon, of November, within Dubrovnik. I have no knowledge of that particular incident that you're talking about because, as I said to you, I wasn't there at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But if we go back to the area of Dubrovnik itself once again, did you say that there was fighting ongoing there too for as long as they lasted, that is, that there was an exchange of fire on both sides?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: When I was there, there was certainly fire into the Dubrovnik area, and there was some fire from the Dubrovnik area, return fire, but not from the old city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Not from the old city. Why do you call the fire coming from Dubrovnik as return fire? Does that mean that the JNA forces fired first and then the Croatian forces responded or was it perhaps the other way round? I've read to you parts of the letter by Admiral Brovet from which it is evident what patience they showed in endeavouring to stop the fire against JNA positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we've been over all this ground. It's pointless going on. You can ask one more question and then your time is up, if you've got something else you want to ask. We've been over this ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, General, do you know that throughout that period that you are talking about, the role of the JNA was precisely to separate forces that were in conflict, and they were conflict because of the violence which the new Croatian authority had committed against the Serb population? Are you aware of that, that the role of the JNA was that, that it endeavoured to separate the warring parties? And the Serbs in Croatia were the party that was attacked. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I was aware that that was the justification given for many of the actions that were taking place, but that was at variance with what actually took place on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kay, have you any questions? Questioned by Mr. Kay:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you were largely based in Zagreb; is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: Based in Zagreb and then we were deployed as teams to areas within Croatia on occasions, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The ECMM, did it have only that main base in Zagreb or did it have other bases or centres, if you like, elsewhere in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: Initially it was in Zagreb, and then they developed a network of centres, what they called Regional Centres, in a number of other locations, first in Croatia and then in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The setup in Belgrade was at what stage? Can you give us an approximate date?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: Approximately the end of October. I'm not sure exactly of the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The arrival of the ECMM to Zagreb, again, approximate date?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: It would have arrived approximately the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived, you were, so to speak, in the Croatian partition of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived, would it be fair to say that you were viewed with suspicion by the other side, the side that was not the Croats?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: Initially -- yes. I would think that that would be fair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that there was no contact or response from the JNA when you were trying to perform your task of implementing a cease-fire, the cessation of hostilities. Again, would it be fair to say from your dealings on the matter that that would have been because the other side viewed you as being partial to the Croatians? Whether that's right or wrong is another matter, it's their perception that I would like you to give evidence about.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I don't think that that would be fair to say, because on a number of other occasions, the JNA did engage with us and cease-fires were arranged. I had personal experience of it in the Osijek area myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can just turn to tab 8, second page, paragraph 6, the Dalmatia section. I take it from the date on page 1, the 14th of October, that this may well have been after you had left Dubrovnik. From your six days, it seems you would have left around the 12th; is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I would have been there from the 5th to the 7th or 8th of October. So I was well gone on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's -- the document date is actually the 11th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it outside your time, this report, or within your time? Just see if you can help us.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: The actual report refers to the changeover time. As you see, the team reports another quiet day. That would have been the team in situ, and then the other team was arriving. So the report covers the period of the handover, as far as I can ascertain from it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 6 reads as follows: "The same team reports that the JNA has for the first time made contact to talk."

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: Yes. That refers to our successor team. I think in my evidence I mentioned that, that the successor team made contact and did have a meeting with the JNA and the Croatian authorities at Cavtat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from the way we read it, it seems as though the JNA made that contact rather than it being the other way around.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: Well, as I say, it was the successor team. I don't know who made the initial contact in that case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving on to other matters, in your period in Zagreb, were you able to receive reports as to the kind of information that was coming out of the media in Croatia itself?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: There would have been a cell at the headquarters there that were receiving media digests from all of the interested parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The issue I just want to look at briefly here is your experience of that, or the ECMM experience of it, and whether there could be any assessment of the kind of reporting that was taking place within Croatia as to the events that were happening. Were those local reports from the Croatia media exaggerations of the hostilities and conflicts?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: There was a dedicated press section at the headquarters who would have had the responsibility of analysing and dissecting the media, so I would feel that it would be -- a comment of that nature would be more appropriate to them than to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But were you aware, rather than having someone else come along, were you aware of those reports that were being made within the Croatia media? I say that because of those comments that were within the document that we withdrew this morning of which you were not the author.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: There were comments made, yes, that like would not have been fully reflective of the facts on the ground, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to deal with this point: That the reports within Croatia as to what was happening were an exaggeration of the real events; is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: I would prefer to say that some of the reports in the Croatian media were an exaggeration of the real events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Gaining an understanding that that was the situation would not be immediate, would that be right, when you and your ECMM team arrive in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: That would be correct, yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It takes time to work out what the realities are.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: That is correct, but I think pragmatically one would expect the reporting of one particular side or another to be of a rather subjective nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Just one other matter. You referred to one of these tabs, it may even have been this one, as going to The Hague. I didn't quite understand the context of that.

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: At that particular time, the Dutch had the presidency of the EU, and the Dutch presidency then received the reports and circulated them to all of the other participating countries at that time. They had that responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I have a few questions. Re-examined by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in relation to your information on the imminent attack on Dubrovnik, the accused put to you whether this was in fact preparation for a future provocation against the JNA. Did you see anything in Dubrovnik when you were there that could justify such a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The accused also spoke with you about the amount of fire from the Croatian side in Dubrovnik, and you yourself spoke about what you saw and heard. Would that what you saw and heard coming from the Croatian side, would it justify the bombardment from the JNA that you saw?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: No, it would not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The accused also spoke with you about the agreement of the -- of the 13th of July, 1991, and mentioned is here - and he pointed this out in particular - the lifting of the blockade of the JNA units and facilities, but it also says here "the unconditional return of the JNA units to their barracks." Did the JNA, to your information -- to your knowledge, did they return unconditionally to their barracks?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And returning to blockades of barracks and the Dubrovnik scenario, was in Dubrovnik any barracks of the JNA blockaded?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: Not in the Dubrovnik area to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Prevlaka, was Prevlaka threatened? The JNA in Prevlaka, were they threatened?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us that you could not see any military reason for what was going on in Dubrovnik. What did you believe at that time was the reason for what you saw going on in Dubrovnik and what also continued after you left?

utterances.speaker: COLM MANGAN
utterances.text: It was not apparent to me what reason the attack was going on in the Dubrovnik area, because as I have stated in my evidence, if the JNA had wanted to take Dubrovnik, at that time it was so lightly defended it would have been a very simple matter for them but they didn't do it. Consequently, I was mystified.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: General, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, there is one matter, formal matter. We were asked, with that last witness, and apparently the same thing happened to the witness before, although I did not note -- did not take action at the time, we were asked to mark the proofing summary for identification. Now, that has not been our practice, as I recollect. We've not admitted the proofing summaries, they having a totally different function, and at the moment, I'm not minded -- I don't think we're minded, rather - I speak for the Trial Chamber - to admit this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The reason I think I'd mentioned it on two previous occasions is simply if at any later stage there was any need to know what was in a proofing summary and it's not marked for identification there could be some difficulty or confusion. If something's referred to in, for example, a passage of examination or cross-examination by reference to a proofing summary, a later review of the materials without the proofing summary would be a little difficult to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There haven't been any -- there haven't been any references in the last witness to the witness summary. I would rather that we kept the proofing summaries out, because it only adds to confusion, quite honestly. If an issue arises, the proofing summary no doubt you will retain and you can produce when need be. So we will not mark those for identification. And that will also apply to the ambassador's evidence where we seem to have marked one for identification. We will remove them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If Your Honour pleases. We made good progress this morning in time. The ambassador is due to come back, obviously immediately. Before he does, a word about witness lists in light of the accused's concerns. He may be confusing two types of witness lists. The regular witness list, notifying him of next week's witnesses, is being provided today. The other witness list, to which I was referring, was the witness list which would be part of the discussion about procedure and timetable. I'm just informed that it's pretty well in final shape. It's just being reviewed. Although I shan't be here myself tomorrow we can have it at least provided in courtesy copies, if that would help the Trial Chamber over the weekend and indeed the accused, because I think procedural matters must proceed next week. If the ambassador's evidence is not -- doesn't take all of the remainder of today and tomorrow, there's then a question of what to do with the balance of tomorrow, because as I say, unfortunately, I shan't be here, cannot be here. It may be we'll revert to Mr. Blewitt, who is our most available filler witness. I don't think it's going to be possible to go into one of next week's witnesses and advance them to tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be that we can go back to the Rule 92 bis witnesses, which we still have a great number to get through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: My learned friends can deal with those, yes, in my absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It might be sensible to do that tomorrow. We'll have to see how long the ambassador is needed for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Otherwise, I am very anxious that I should lay out the position about procedure and finish the financial argument --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can do that on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I would hope so, yes. Well, we can't do it on Monday. Absolutely it's a question of putting back the first witness perhaps to the second session on Monday and hoping to conclude that witness and the other witness by the end of Tuesday, but if we can't finish them by Tuesday, one of them will have to come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are they -- do you know if they are substantial witnesses, either of these?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The first one is an expert, producing a number of exhibits, so his examination-in-chief should not be particularly substantial, and of course cross-examination will have to allow for the fact that his material has gone in under the provisions of an expert witness. The second one I'm not sure at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which expert is he?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Grujic. Mr. Grujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff will deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Colonel Grujic is the head of the commission of the Croats for missing and detained and killed people, and he will provide a lot of statistical documentation on missing people, detained people, killed people related to the indictment, the Croatia indictment. This is the subject of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And it's a huge amount of documents, but we think we can get it in in a summarising fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I was going to say, you're not going to take very long, then, in chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No. He has provided an expert report and I would only address a few matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What about the other witnesses? Is that a long one? It may be it's a Bosnia witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He deals with a number of detention camps. He's likely to be quite substantial. And it simply may be that he'll have to return from whence he came and come back again after our five-day break, or is it six-day break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Since we must deal with these administrative matters and not put them off, it would be sensible to take the first session on Monday, then, on those and put the witnesses back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll try and provide -- or, we will provide by way of courtesy copies the charts and lists that I'm going to refer to on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I didn't follow well. What expertise does he have, Mr. Grujic?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: He's the head of the commission who dealt with all these matters, and he's also -- he was present during exhumation proceedings and those kind of the matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that you will order them to give me a list of witnesses so that the practice is for me to know at least a week in advance which witnesses will be testifying for purposes of my cross-examination, because surprises seem to be sprung all the time, and it is not possible, with this mass of documents that the opposite side is endeavouring to inundate me with, for me to identify overnight and to read through the statements to see what it's all about. So I can't understand, with the enormous apparatus that they have at their disposal they're not in a position to give me a proper list of witnesses for one week in advance, a valid list of witnesses and that they should adhere to. And also I think that this practice of interrupting one witness, putting another one in his stead leads to confusion. We had Okun yesterday and then the general and then the cross-examination and now we're going to carry on with Okun, and so on and so forth. And I also wish to say that I don't understand what time you're talking about tomorrow, because yesterday Okun testified throughout the working day, and today, as far as I'm able to gather, he will be continuing and completing his testimony. Perhaps I shall be able to start my cross-examination, but I assume that I have the rest of tomorrow at my disposal for it. Is that right? The whole day tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will see. Yesterday, you may remember, was a short day, it was only three hours. But you're right that he testified for those three hours. We will add, of course, the time which he's testifying today, and we'll consider the matter. As for the interposing of witnesses, that is not a practice which is encouraged, but occasionally when you have a witness such as the last one who has important public duties to fulfil, it's important that this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Tribunal tries to fit those duties in as far as possible. And although it's inconvenient from the point of view of the trial, sometimes the witness's convenience has to come first, but obviously it's a practice which should be kept to a minimum. But let me inquire this: What the accused is certainly entitled to is a list for the week after next so that he can prepare during the break for that list. For the next two weeks, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That will be provided to him. It comes, of course, with the necessary caution that things can change for reasons outside our control, but yes, we'll provide that to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be convenient to deal with one other matter. You asked us yesterday to consider Witness C-032, I think was the number, who is a military witness, and you ask in your application that he be allowed to deal with some matters by way of Rule 92 bis. They are matters concerned with various laws, and I must say they appear to me - to us - to be admissible under Rule 92 bis, but of course we'll have to hear. Mr. Kay, anything you want to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. The Trial Chamber has given its initial ruling on Rule 92 bis and there are no observations we have on this matter, this aspect of that witness's evidence, and that's why we haven't put in a written document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. If you don't want to put in a written document, just address us orally on all these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. There's no comment we have on that or, for that matter, Rousseau, who was the third addendum, because they've picked out the areas which are suitable for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And they're not in way connected with the acts or conduct of the accused or for any other reason not admissible. Mr. Milosevic, anything you want to say about this witness, C-032? He will be called to give evidence but his statement will be admitted for those paragraphs which I've identified.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand the question, Mr. May. If you're referring to the testimony pursuant to 92 bis, then I -- you know that I am against the use and application of that Rule, because it shortens everything to a great measure and diminishes the possibility for the -- for verifying the facts that are being presented. You heard the general a moment ago. I had no objection to make or comments to his priority. I know that he is Chief of the General Staff the Irish army and that therefore he has his duties to attend to. And you heard the general who rejected certain portions of what was provided here. So when we follow Rule 92 bis, it is quite unclear whether it is a statement by the witness or something written by the opposite side over there. And that's the crux of the matter. The second point is that I have very limited time for cross-examining witnesses that are pursuant to that Rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. As for any suggestion that the statement is written by the Prosecutor or the investigator, that is a suggestion which is to be rejected. If that practice was going on, then it's a matter which we would have to look into. But it's not suggested that that is so here. Your general objection you made before. We bear in mind the amount of time which you should have in cross-examination depending on the nature of the evidence, and so that is catered for. We will admit the statement under Rule 92 business, those paragraphs which appear in the application.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're obliged. The Chamber will remember that when we first dealt with the first 92 bis, or partly bis'd, witness, we reviewed in a public way the process by which 92 bis is applied. It may be appropriate, in light of the accused's suggestion or allegation, it may be appropriate with the next 92 bis witness simply to remind those viewing, through testimony, how the 92 process -- 92 bis process actually takes place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now, and we will continue with the evidence of the ambassador in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Groome: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, when we concluded yesterday, you were discussing or describing to the Chamber the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. I'm going to ask that you be shown tab 10 of Prosecution Exhibit 396 now. I'd ask you to identify it, if you're able.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is that document?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the text of the political section of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. There was also a military annex which is not in this document --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- concerning military dispositions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Can you describe for us Mr. Milosevic's position regarding the Vance-Owen Peace Plan.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my judgement, Mr. Milosevic favoured the plan. I say that based primarily on a lengthy meeting that Lord Owen and I held with President Milosevic in Belgrade, I believe towards the end of April 1993, at which he -- or to which, I should say, excuse me, to which he summoned Radovan Karadzic, and in our presence they discussed the plan, and President Milosevic spoke in its favour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you believe his efforts to advocate on behalf of the plan to be sincere efforts?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They appeared to be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I'm going to ask you to comment briefly on what you can tell the Chamber regarding the relationship between the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, the Yugoslav army, the VJ, and the army of the Republika Srpska, or the VRS, and I would direct the Chamber's attention to paragraph 72 of the summary. Could you briefly describe for us what you know about this relationship that you learned from your official duties at this time.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The relationship between the JNA, the Bosnian Serb army, which was its successor in Bosnia, were very close, were intimate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe the -- in a little greater detail what you know about the nature of that relationship, both prior to the withdrawal of the JNA in Bosnia and subsequent to their withdrawal.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the JNA, for historic and geographic reasons, regarded Bosnia and Herzegovina as its heartland. This stemmed from the World War II experience where the partisan movement was based primarily in Bosnia and most of the fighting against the German occupying forces took place in Bosnia. Tito declared the existence of the Republic in Jajce in November 1943, in Bosnia, and there were a host of other reasons. Additionally, for geographic reasons, much of former Yugoslavia's military industrial complex was located in Bosnia-Herzegovina since it was in the centre of the country. At the time of the cessation of hostilities in Croatia, the JNA had probably between 90 and 100.000 troops already stationed in Bosnia. They were to withdraw from Croatia, as we've already discussed, and by the time -- or I should say when the fighting began to occur in May -- in March of 1992 in Bosnia, the JNA probably had some something like 80, 90.000 soldiers there still. In May of 1992, the JNA officially withdrew, or formally withdrew. This was a paper withdrawal because in fact they did not withdraw from Croatia until October 1992. But there was a withdrawal in May of 1992. So at that point, the JNA was in Bosnia. It was later renamed the VJ, the army of Yugoslavia. And again at that time, the Bosnian Serb army, the VRS, was technically created. But what happened was, in English, to put it plainly and leave the initials out of it, the JNA in effect became the VRS, the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this was visible to us, because the gasoline, the ammunition came from Serbia across the river, across the Drina into Bosnia. This was no secret to anybody. After all, to maintain 80 or 90.000 fighting troops in the field requires quite a lot of logistic support.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you become aware of who was paying the salaries of the officers in the VRS army?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were widely informed, although I have no direct personal knowledge of the fact, but we were widely informed that the salaries of the Bosnian Serb army, that is the VRS, were paid by the Defence Ministry in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then, Ambassador, if you can, could you comment on any knowledge you have regarding General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I met him several times, and I know of his reputation as well. He had been the commander of the Knin Corps in Croatia, Knin being the most sensitive and most Serb area on the territory of Croatia, and so that position was already an important one. He was widely said to be the most popular JNA officer in the army, and particularly popular with the troops, that is the enlisted men. He was even referred to as the George Patton of the JNA, George Patton being a famous American general from the Second World War. As I say, I also met him on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador, how many pages altogether are the diaries that you've been referring to during the course of your testimony? An approximate number.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Close to 2.000, I should say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, in the course of your preparation to testify here, did you work with a member of the OTP staff to make some charts identifying the most relevant entries into the diaries?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I'm going to ask that Prosecution Exhibit 396, tab 11, a demonstrative exhibit, be placed on the overhead projector. I'm going to ask that the usher push the "off" switch on the witness's console. And just a word of explanation: I will ask Ambassador Okun to identify the most relevant diary entries. The diary entries themselves will appear on the Sanction screen, and the demonstrative exhibit will remain on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I'd ask you -- and I might add that the demonstrative exhibits have been attached at the back of the witness summary that the Chamber, Mr. Milosevic, and the amici have. Ambassador, this first chart, does this chart indicate some of the more relevant entries regarding Mr. Milosevic's relationship to paramilitary organisations?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you to begin with the first entry and to summarise the entry. The entry should appear on the screen in front of you if you want to refer to it. Of course, feel free to go to the original notebooks if you need. If it's a meeting that we have discussed already, I'd ask you just to refer us back to your earlier testimony regarding that meeting.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if I may. The first meeting is dated 18 November 1991. We've already discussed it here in this court. And it concerns President Milosevic's assurance to Secretary Vance that in Serbia - and here I paraphrase - in Serbia irregular or paramilitary troops are not allowed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. The next item, please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next item is 21 November 1991, also mentioned in previous testimony. The president informed Secretary Vance that we would have no problem with the withdrawal of the JNA or Serbian irregulars from Croatia with regard to the peacekeeping plan. The next item --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps there's been some misunderstanding, Mr. Okun. On the 21st, it says, "When Vance informed [In English] Milosevic that Kadijevic was ready to withdraw the JNA from Croatia, Milosevic told him," et cetera. [Interpretation] That means that Vance informed me that Kadijevic was ready to withdraw the JNA. I did not inform Vance. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can clarify that in cross-examination, if you need to, but since you've raised the matter now, yes, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, President. You confirmed the withdrawal. You were confirming the withdrawal. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 23 November 1991, President Milosevic, again as we know from previous discussion in this room, signed the Geneva Accord, which bound all armed Serbian forces, including Serbian paramilitaries and irregulars, and nobody from the Federal Presidency signed the document, therefore indicating that President Milosevic's signature was controlling for the Federal Presidency as well. Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 2nd of December, 1991, when Secretary Vance asked the president -- asked the president about the paramilitaries' reaction to the cease-fire, President Milosevic informed him that they were observing the cease-fire, having already told us that 95 per cent of the Serb paramilitaries were organised and under the control of Goran Hadzic. On 15 April 1992, a meeting which we have already discussed in this Chamber, a meeting in which Secretary Vance strongly adverted to President Milosevic about Arkan's continued activities, President Milosevic stated - again I paraphrase - that only some individual paramilitaries not under the control of Serbian authorities were active. And that was the meeting after some discussion, Your Honours will recall, that President Milosevic admitted, acknowledged to us that Arkan had been in Bijeljina at the beginning of the fighting, and it was our contention that he had been in other places as well. On the 5th of June, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it 6th of May?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ambassador, for this chart we use the European convention of day, month, year, as opposed to the American convention.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. On the 6th of May, 1992, President Milosevic committed himself to Secretary Vance. He made the commitment that the paramilitaries, by which all understood Serb paramilitaries, would be out of Bosnia, that is withdrawn from Bosnia-Herzegovina within two weeks. And the quote was: "All Serbs and the JNA will be out of Bosnia-Herzegovina in two weeks." I think we've also discussed that here previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I ask now that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 396, tab 12.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, does this chart summarise the most significant diary entries relevant to Mr. Milosevic's relationship to the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you to guide us through this demonstrative exhibit now.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first entry, dated 13 October 1991, we've already discussed. This was the meeting at which General Kadijevic, the Federal Secretary of Defence, told us that the JNA did not act independently, followed the orders of the Rump Presidency, that its chains of command were intact, and it had no rogue elements. The next item, dated 6 November 1991, records the Prime Minister, the Federal Prime Minister, Ante Markovic, informing us that the JNA was becoming increasingly more Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did we deal with that phrase during the testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we have already, Your Honour, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The third item, dated 18 November 1991 --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, before you leave that comment that the JNA was becoming increasingly more Serbian, did you, during the course of your negotiations, learn the reasons behind or the forces that were resulting in the JNA becoming more Serbianised?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you explain that to the Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. There were several factors that caused the JNA to become more Serbian. The first and primary factor was that officers and men of the JNA, of the federal army, who came from the other republics, were increasingly deserting, leaving the JNA to return to their federal republics. I might cite as an example General Anton Tus, who was the Commander-in-Chief of the Croatian armed forces in 1991. He had been previously the commander of the air force of the JNA. And this went on by the thousands when you considered the number of men as well. Additionally, the call-ups, the conscription into the JNA were not answered by the republics that were in succession. And finally, many Serbian lads themselves chose not to answer the call-up. So for these three concurrent reasons, the JNA became increasingly more Serbian and in effect a Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue with the chart, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 18 November 1991, I believe we've discussed previously. This was the meeting at which Secretary Vance made the initial formal proposal suggesting a possible UN peacekeeping operation to President Milosevic, at which meeting the president stated that the Serb side and the JNA would accept and agree to the setting up of a peacekeeping operation. The next item we've already discussed. In its chronological place, this was the meeting that followed directly on the meeting of 18 November with President Milosevic. The meeting that followed it was with General Kadijevic, and he accepted the plan. Three days later, on 21 November, when Secretary Vance informed President Milosevic that General Kadijevic was ready to withdraw the JNA- and I repeat this was Secretary Vance informing the president - the president responded: "Good. You'll have no problem with the JNA or the Serbian irregulars." The next meeting was 23 November 1991. Again this concerns the signature of the unblocking and cease-fire accord in Geneva which bound all Serbian armed forces, including the JNA, and bound the irregulars, and this was the accord that was signed by President Tudjman and by General Kadijevic and by President Milosevic and was not signed by anyone from the Federal Presidency. At that time, as we've previously discussed, Borisav Jovic was the federal president, and he was not even present in Geneva for that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, before you leave that point, leading up to the signing of the Geneva Accord, did Secretary Vance or yourself have any substantive discussions or negotiations with Borisav Jovic himself regarding the terms of the Geneva Accord?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. I believe Secretary Vance did not. But I recall, and there's a diary entry, a meeting of the federal unit that was preparing to receive the peacekeeping operation. President Milosevic suggested that I meet with that unit to explain to them the conditions, and I did so. And it was a rather large meeting in a big hall. There was 25 or 30 people around a large table. And Mr. Jovic was the leader of the meeting at the Yugoslav side. I don't believe Secretary Vance ever dealt with or had more than a handshake with Mr. Jovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The penultimate item on that page, 2 December 1991, we've already discussed, and this indicates President Milosevic's response to Secretary Vance's question about Dalmatia and the fighting along the coast. The president said that once the JNA garrison was unblocked, the army would leave Dubrovnik alone. The final item on this page, dated 6 May 1992, concerns the meeting we've discussed a few moments ago, namely President Milosevic's commitment to Secretary Vance that the JNA would depart from Bosnia within two weeks, and it lists his statement already discussed that Bosnia and Herzegovina were not within the competence of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I ask now that the ambassador be shown Prosecution Exhibit 396, tab 13.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I'd ask you, does this demonstrative aid indicate those most significant diary entries describing the relationship between Mr. Milosevic and other Serb political leaders?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you if you could walk us through this chart.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first item, dated 12 October 1991, I believe has not been previously discussed in this court with me. It concerns the statement -- it describes the statement of the then Federal Foreign Minister Loncar, who told us that the Serbian government was insisting on the right to speak for the Serbs in Croatia. Loncar himself is a Croat. The next meeting, dated 18 November 1991, we've discussed. It itemises President Milosevic's statement to Secretary Vance that we would not have any problem with the Krajina leadership of Milan Babic and Goran Hadzic, and he added, "Believe me." Item number 3 concerns the meeting of 21 November 1991, already discussed here, at which President Milosevic told us once again that we would not have problems with Hadzic. And when Secretary Vance asked for maps and a list of places where Serbs lived, the president said he would have Hadzic provide them for him. The next item, in two parts, dated December 2, 1991, relates to the discussion between President Milosevic, Secretary Vance, and myself, in which the president stated that he had already spoken with both Milan Babic and Goran Hadzic on the day after the signing of the accord of Geneva. That day would have been 24 November 1991. And the president said they would observe the cease-fire. Referring to himself, President Milosevic said to Mr. Vance and to me, "I promised and I did." Meaning, of course, that, "I promised you I would speak with Hadzic and Babic, and I did so." Later in that same meeting, and this we have already discussed, President Milosevic suggested that we talk to the Bosnian Serb leaders. We were given the name of Karadzic as the person who speak with. We asked for a meeting, and a few hours later we met with Dr. Radovan Karadzic at a house in a Belgrade residential neighbourhood. The next meeting, dated 31 December 1991, the last day of the year, contains a typographical error. May I inform the Court of it? The date of the implementing accord is 2 January, not 7 January. That date has already been given to the Court and is contained in the documents. It is a mere typographical error. In any case, as the date for the signing of the implementing accord of 2 January drew near, we asked the president what could happen if another Krajina leader like Babic might appear. The reason for that question was that Babic was very recalcitrant initially in terms of accepting the cease-fire, and the question was to elicit the guarantee, if you will, from President Milosevic that that would not occur again, that the paramilitaries and the political leaders, the political military leaders in the Krajina, were under his control. And the president assured us that would not happen. He assured us there would be no new Babic. The penultimate item on that page, dated 4 March 1992, I believe we've not discussed previously. It states that President Milosevic told Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Secretary Vance --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, since we have not discussed this, please feel free to look at the entire diary entry, if you wish, and to go into a little greater detail regarding what occurred during that meeting.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's the 4th of March, 1992. And that would be in book 6, page 92.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. This was a discussion of more than three hours with President Milosevic. It covered many subjects, including the JNA, which we discussed a moment ago. And I note on page 90 parenthetically that President Milosevic told us correctly that the JNA was being reduced in size. This relates back to the question I was asked previously as to the changing composition of the JNA, and we discussed the departure from the JNA of troops from the various republics, and President Milosevic told us it was being reduced in size. Most of the discussion, however, concerned the worsening situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Again, this date was the 3rd of April, 1992. The fighting had been under way for about a month by this time, and it was getting worse and worse, and indeed, the ethnic cleansing was getting worse. And when Secretary Vance raised this problem, President Milosevic agreed that it was a problem and said that he wished to discuss it privately with Secretary Vance and then stated, on the top of page 92: "I called Karadzic and told him to cool it." In other words, "I called Radovan Karadzic and told him to slow down, cease his activities, not be so warlike." I mean, "cool it" is a perfectly acceptable somewhat informal expression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The final item on the page is dated 2 October 1992. We have not discussed this, I believe, previously in the Chamber. It concerns the possible imposition of a no-fly zone over Bosnia.
